analysis.one_liner: Bans PACs from federal elections and cuts the individual contribution limit.
analysis.headline: The PAC-ban bill died without ever getting a vote: it was referred to the House Administration Committee on the day it was introduced in January 1993 and never came out of committee in the two years before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the federal campaign finance law to bar political action committees — the committees funded by corporations, trade associations, and labor unions — from contributing to or spending money on federal elections. It also would have cut the limit on what an individual person can give to a candidate from $1,000 to $500, pushing candidates toward many small donors instead of a few large ones. It was introduced on the first day of the 103rd Congress and sent to the House Administration Committee, where it sat until that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters would gain a campaign finance system in which candidates raise money from individual citizens rather than from PACs funded by corporate, trade association, and labor treasuries. Smaller-dollar donors would gain relative influence, since the individual limit would drop from $1,000 to $500. Candidates without access to PAC networks would benefit from a system that no longer compares their small-donor totals to rivals' PAC hauls.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new section to the Federal Election Campaign Act providing that no person other than an individual or a political committee may contribute, solicit or receive contributions, or make expenditures to influence a federal election — a broad prohibition that would strip PACs of any role in federal campaigns [S3].

It cuts the individual contribution limit to candidates from $1,000 to $500, so a candidate could not rely on a small pool of maximum-dollar donors and would have to build broad small-donor support [S3] [S2].

The CRS summary describes the bill as prohibiting federal election activities by political action committees and reducing the candidate contribution ceiling by persons other than multicandidate political committees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate, trade association, and labor PACs would lose their ability to fund federal candidates, and the industries and unions that use PACs to buy access and goodwill with lawmakers would lose that channel. Incumbent members of Congress — who are among the largest recipients of PAC money — would have to replace PAC dollars with individual donations of no more than $500 each.

drawbacks.text: Critics of strict contribution limits argue that banning PACs and cutting individual limits to $500 does not reduce the demand for campaign money but pushes it into less regulated channels — party soft money, independent expenditures, and candidates' personal wealth — potentially weakening disclosure and helping wealthy self-funded candidates over grassroots ones. This concern is a general policy argument, not drawn from the bill's record [S3].

A total PAC ban is blunt: it removes a channel that at least operates under contribution limits and public disclosure, without replacing it with public financing or any other source of campaign funds, so the bill's practical effect depends on where the money goes next [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacked a real problem — PAC money gives organized corporate and labor interests a routine channel to the lawmakers who regulate them — and its individual limit cut pushes toward broad small-donor fundraising. But it was a one-sided restriction with no replacement funding source, and serious reformers acknowledge that caps this tight risk driving money into unregulated channels. Even so, the main cost falls on organized interests and incumbent fundraisers, not on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Romano Mazzoli of Kentucky introduced the bill on January 5, 1993, the opening day of the 103rd Congress, joined by Rep. David Poshard [S3] [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over campaign finance law [S5] [S1].
No further action is listed in the bill's history: it never left committee, never reached the House floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5] [S1].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors in two years, so it never built the support needed to force the committee to act [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs and the corporate and labor interests that fund them, along with incumbent members of Congress who draw on PAC money, were better off because the bill never moved — the PAC system they rely on stayed untouched.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got to a vote, so no roll call shows how parties would have split; it had two Democratic cosponsors and died in a Democratic-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, trade association, and labor)
industries.note: The bill would have banned PACs entirely from federal elections, eliminating their ability to give to candidates and spend on campaigns. PACs exist to channel organizational money to the lawmakers who regulate their funders, so their interest in surviving runs against a campaign finance system built on individual donors.

Incumbents are major recipients of PAC money, so a ban would cut off a reliable funding stream; but incumbents also benefit from the visibility and organizational advantages PACs provide. The committee that buried the bill is run by members of Congress deciding the rules for their own fundraising.

industries.industry: Corporate and union treasuries using PACs for political access
industries.note: Companies and unions would have lost a direct, structured route to fund federal candidates and gain goodwill with them. The alternative — raising money from individual citizens in $500 increments — is far more labor-intensive for organized interests.
